title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
author: Melody Zixuan Li, Taylor Webb
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.

title: Measuring Definition Sensitivity in LLM Annotation of Social Science Concepts
author: Bogdan Mamaev, Qizhou Wang, Christopher Leckie, Matteo Vergani
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In social science research, text annotation is a fundamental task that is traditionally a costly, hard-to-scale manual process. Researchers have used large language models (LLMs) to perform annotation by writing a definition of a concept into a prompt - a rule that determines whether a label should be attributed to a text depending on its content. However, concepts such as hate speech, fake news, and terrorism typically have several theoretically defensible competing definitions. It is also unknown whether the model actually applied the definition to provide the label or the label was based on the model's pretrained notion of the concept. To test this, we have the model annotate the same texts twice, each time with a different definition. We call the disagreement between the two sets of annotations definition sensitivity. As a control, we paraphrase one definition but leave its requirements unchanged - the disagreement between the annotations with the two wordings becomes the paraphrase floor. Across six concepts and three LLMs, a swap of competing definitions always changes more annotations, on average, than a paraphrase. This shows that the annotations depend on the prompted definition, so any set of annotations should be interpreted together with the definition that produced it. The LLM annotator's definition sensitivity and its paraphrase floor should both be reported in such work.

title: Understanding Students' Rationales for AI-Mediated Cheating: An Instructor Perspective from Online Forums Analysis
author: Iman Mohammadi, Sina Rismanchian, Ali Keramati, Shayan Salehi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The extensive adoption of AI has precipitated a crisis in academic integrity. While studies attempt to quantify cheating, less is known about the motivations instructors believe students have for using AI in prohibited ways. We analyze 2.01 million posts on r/Professors to understand how instructors perceive students' justifications for AI-mediated cheating. Our qualitative analyses reveal four primary themes: (1) Academic System Gaming, (2) Digital-Academic Literacy Gap, (3) Performance Anxiety, and (4) Normalization of Dishonesty.

title: Mapping Instructors' Attitudes Towards Cheating with AI: An Exploratory Analysis Using Forum Analysis
author: Iman Mohammadi, Ali Keramati, Sina Rismanchian
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In teaching and learning environments, cheating and the violation of academic integrity have always been one of the challenges, involving different levels of concerns such as administrative, personal knowledge, learning, and equity. The introduction of large language models has brought cheating in dialogue to the forefront, given the apparent capabilities of these models to complete students' academic assignments. This study aims to leverage recent dialogues among university professors about cheating with Generative AI to better understand their beliefs about academic honesty. In doing so, we analyze a corpus of 2.01 million posts (threads and comments) in the r/Professors subreddit discussing cheating after the release of ChatGPT, providing a better understanding of teachers' motivations to discourage cheating and the strategies they use to do so. We synthesize the why and how of addressing cheating to identify caveats about the future of AI and academic integration.

title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
author: Mingchen Li, Yongkang Xiao, Rumeng Li, Rui Zhang, Hong Yu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.

title: Inherited Weights: Measuring the Tokenization Premium and the Sovereignty Cost of Language Models for the Global South
author: Paulo Camara (LUA Vision)
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. We argue that fine-tuning leaves the decisive properties of a model inherited from its base: vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license. We contribute (i) an updated, reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers released in 2023-2024, on 27 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with explicit correction for unknown-token collapse. Premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain at 6.8x in the newest commercial one; Indigenous South American languages pay between 1.6x and 2.7x under global tokenizers. A vocabulary built from Portuguese lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages relative to every global tokenizer tested, by about 24% for Guarani and Quechua. (ii) An eight-test black-box sovereignty audit that a buyer can run without access to weights. (iii) A regime argument: under energy and liability constraints, accuracy per joule, calibration and selective risk should replace raw accuracy as design objectives, with metrics that abstention cannot inflate. We close with preliminary internal measurements from a proprietary architecture built around these objectives, reported with their limitations. Data and measurement code are included.

title: An ensemble of graph generative models for assisted history matching of the Brugge field case
author: Gleb Shishaev, Anton Shirokov, Shadfar Davoodi, Mohammed Al-Shargabi, Vasily Demyanov, Daniel Arnold
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assisted history matching remains non-unique because many geological realisations can reproduce equivalent production responses with substantial differences between individual well matches. This ambiguity increases when a field comprises several depositional settings and modelling strategies. The paper applied a graph autoencoder approach to history matching of a benchmark Brugge field that comprises different depositional zones. Each stratigraphic zone is modelled with its dedicated generative model that comprises a joint latent space for optimisation history matching loops. Graph-based generators operate directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, so its irregular geometry is handled without conversion to a regular lattice. The optimisation search in the 160-dimensional joint latent space is done with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. The multi-component objective function includes static well data mismatch, dynamic production mismatch, and a geological realism penalty based on the Decoder induced latent metric. Latent space diagnostics with topological data analysis are applied prior to history matching to test whether one generator is sufficient or whether a multiple generator formulation is required. The results show that the zone-based formulation gives coherent latent spaces, preserves the main porosity and permeability relations that vary from one zone to another, and supports history matching while keeping the solutions within the learned geological manifold. The matched models reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range and provide a comparable well-level match to previously published Brugge studies based on Ensemble Kalman Filter, Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation, and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation.

title: ADIndex: Layer-Adaptive Sparse Attention Indexing via Group-Level Distillation
author: Jin-Fei Qi, Yiduo Li, Jiang-Xin Shi, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Hanlin Tang, Yu-Feng Li
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.

title: Exploration via Exploitation: The Blessing of Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL
author: Jiin Woo, Gauri Joshi, Yuejie Chi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While federated reinforcement learning (RL) has traditionally guaranteed high efficiency in homogeneous environments, collaboration is often hindered when agents possess distinct goals. In this paper, we flip this paradigm, framing reward heterogeneity not as a hurdle to consensus, but as a structural asset that catalyzes exploration. We first propose Personalized Federated Upper Confidence Bound Value Iteration (PF-UCBVI), which achieves optimal linear speedup by decoupling shared dynamics from personalized objectives. To eliminate the risks of explicit exploration, we then introduce Personalized Federated Exploration-Free Value Iteration (PF-EFVI), a purely greedy algorithm that leverages reward diversity to ensure state-action coverage. We prove that PF-EFVI attains logarithmic regret without explicit exploration bonuses under sufficient reward diversity. Our results reveal that agent disagreement shifts the exploration burden from temporal complexity to spatial diversity, enabling efficient collective learning without explicit exploration.

title: StatPrompt-LLM: A Lightweight Statistical Refinement for Foundation-Style Time-Series Forecasting
author: Aniket Sinha, Veronica W. Tsou
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series forecasting has recently seen a paradigm shift with the introduction of foundation-style models that adapt large pretrained language architectures to sequential data. However, effectively exposing fundamental temporal structures, such as trend, scale, and temporal dependence, to these models remains an open challenge, particularly when the available observations are limited. In this paper, we conduct an exploratory empirical study across different generations of forecasting architectures and propose StatPrompt-LLM, a lightweight statistical refinement of Time-LLM. StatPrompt-LLM augments the existing Time-LLM prompting mechanism with dataset-level statistical information and introduces a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass as a complementary linear forecasting pathway. We evaluate our framework on electricity and meteorological time-series benchmarks, including ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather, under full-prefix and reduced-prefix configurations. Under the 10% reduced-prefix configuration, StatPrompt-LLM achieved lower in-sample prediction errors than Time-LLM, with unweighted average relative reductions across datasets of 40.2% in MSE and 21.4% in MAE. Full-prefix results were more dataset-dependent. Ablation analyses revealed relatively modest and dataset-dependent changes when selected additional statistical descriptor groups were masked within the combined architecture. Computational profiling indicated additional model parameters and runtime overhead relative to Time-LLM.

title: MADSNet: A Multi-Scale Axial-Attentive Dense Spiking Network for Spike Camera Image Reconstruction
author: Sirui Li, Rui Zhao, Siqi Cai, Haizhou Li, Tiejun Huang, Yajing Zheng
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spike cameras encode dynamic scenes into high-temporal-resolution binary spike streams for efficient high-speed vision. Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) can process such signals with sparse and accumulate-only computation, existing SNN-based reconstruction methods are typically shallow and still lag behind ANN-based models in reconstruction fidelity. This paper proposes MADSNet, a Multi-scale Axial-attentive Dense Spiking Network for spike camera image reconstruction. MADSNet adopts a hierarchical spiking encoder--decoder, where a multi-scale spike stem extracts early features, axial spike attention captures long-range dependencies, a dense spiking bottleneck enhances feature reuse, and a spike-to-continuous decoder reconstructs continuous intensity images from spike-domain representations. Experiments on gray-scale and color spike reconstruction show that MADSNet outperforms SSIR by 4.3 dB PSNR and Spk2ImgNet by 1.94 dB on SREDS. Compared with Spk2ImgNet, it achieves about 15$\times$ lower latency and uses only about 1/40 of the estimated energy, demonstrating that carefully designed SNN architectures can improve reconstruction quality while preserving computational efficiency.

title: Third Eye: Beyond Immediate Gains in Recursive Self-Improvement
author: Sujato Dutta, Padala Indira Sneha, Kypu Mahitha, Shashank Vanga, Neeraj Choudhary
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.

title: Multimodal Graph Learning: A Survey of Models, Benchmarks, and Frontiers
author: Rui Xue, Tianfu Wu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which nodes carry text, images, and other modalities while edges encode relations among entities, underlie e-commerce, social media, content platforms, and creative applications. Learning on MAGs has developed along two complementary lines: graph-centric methods redesign how modalities are fused, propagated, and connected within message passing, while foundation-model-centric methods pretrain transferable multimodal graph encoders or bring graph context into multimodal large language models for prediction and generation. In parallel, several benchmarks have appeared with different datasets and evaluation protocols. This survey takes an algorithm-centric and evaluation-grounded view of the field and makes three contributions. Modeling: we introduce a unified message-passing formulation and organize methods into five integration levels (feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation model), covering discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models; within this formulation we derive representative methods as special cases, compare their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates otherwise similar architectures. Datasets and evaluation: we review recent benchmarks, summarize their datasets and metrics, define model-independent descriptors (label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance), and map each evaluation protocol to the baselines it uses. Frontiers: we connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents, covering the multimodal graphs that agents perceive and remember and graph engineering, the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs; we then discuss open problems, concrete efforts for the community, and research directions, including when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models.

title: Linear Probes to Bayesian Manifolds: Geometry of Arithmetic in Large Language Models
author: Anshul Kumar, Neha Prasad, Manoj Kumar, Barnab\'as P\'oczos, Deeksha Varshney
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.12998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear probes are a standard method to study geometric structures, such as helices and circles, from the activations of large language models (LLMs), and such structure is often taken as evidence that the model computes with it. Probe accuracy alone cannot establish this, because it conflates four separate claims. These are (1) that the concept is decodable from the activations, (2) that they form a specific shape, (3) that the shape belongs to the probed concept rather than to a related concept the model also represents, and (4) that the output of the model depends on the shape. We call these claims decodability, shape, ownership, and causal use, and we test them separately with a four-stage Bayesian pipeline. Stage 2 compares candidate shapes and selects the best one only when its evidence passes a predefined threshold. Stage 3 removes a set of related concepts, specified in advance, and tests whether the shape is owned or inherited. Stage 4 intervenes on the shape to test whether the output of the model depends on it. We apply the pipeline to two-digit addition and multiplication in GPT-J 6B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Pythia 6.9B. Nearly every concept is decodable, but the decoded directions overlap substantially across concepts. Every strongly supported comparison selects a ribbon, which is a helix whose radius changes with the value, or a torus. Of 1,330 cells with an ownership verdict, 19% of shapes are owned and 81% are inherited. Owned and inherited shapes move the output about equally often. Intervening on the shape retains approximately 61% of the effect of intervening on the full probe while using at most five dimensions, against a median of nine for the probe. Our results indicate that a probe verdict alone overstates what a model computes with, and we propose that probe results be reported as verdicts on all four claims rather than as a single accuracy.

title: One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction
author: Yuanrui Wang, Kaifang Li, Xuanyue Li, Ziyun Li, Yan Lu, Xingxuan Zhang, Peng Cui
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (\ours{}), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient's own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility--fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

title: Branch-and-Commit for Frozen RL Agents: When and Where to Spend Test-Time Compute
author: Sahar Admoni, Assaf Hallak, Yftah Ziser, Ofra Amir
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning agents are often deployed with policies that cannot be retrained or modified. In digital environments whose states can be copied and resumed, an operator has another option: sample several continuations from the current state, evaluate them, and continue from the endpoint of the selected branch. We call this procedure branch-and-commit. We study when it improves return, what produces the improvement, and where its computational budget should be spent. Across four environments, two frozen policies, five continuation verifiers, and a model-free selection rule, we find that the benefit of branching depends on dispersion: the difference between the best candidate return and the mean candidate return. Branching provides no benefit in low-dispersion settings, while increasing return by 12.8% in our main Craftax-Medium setting. Most of this gain comes not from selecting better actions, but from selecting among different stochastic realizations of the same action. Several competent verifiers achieve similar episode returns, suggesting that verifier quality is not the main constraint at our operating budget. Instead, computation is better allocated to states where useful dispersion is likely. On held-out seeds, gating branching using predicted dispersion retains 69% of the improvement from uniform branching while using 48% as many branching calls. These results characterize when branch-and-commit is useful and clarify what its gains represent.

title: The Shape of a Program: Path Signatures for Trace-to-Program Induction
author: Mohamed Ghanem, Bernd Finkbeiner
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthesizing programs from execution traces is a fundamental challenge in algorithmic interpretability and the reverse engineering of complex systems. We bring a rough-path-theoretic perspective to program induction, treating execution traces as high-dimensional rough paths and encoding them with the path signature transform, a tool from stochastic analysis whose expectation provably characterizes the distribution of traces a program induces. On three program-induction domains, Karel, List, and RASP, our log-signature trace encoder outperforms LSTM, Transformer, and Fourier baselines in almost every setting, with its largest margins when training data is scarce. We further observe that the trace-to-program pipeline is naturally contractive: it often produces valid programs that are shorter than the ground truth. We turn this into a bootstrapping procedure that exposes redundancy in the ground-truth supervision without any external oracle, which we demonstrate on redundancy-injected versions of our datasets. Finally, the log-signature encoder induces a markedly more interpretable latent geometry than the baselines, in which the nearest neighbors of every state lie on its own execution trace.

title: FaST: Factored Synthesis of Transitions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
author: Daniel Campa, Spandan Das, Srinjoy Das
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.

title: Permutation-Based Pre-trained Model Merging via Reciprocal Orthogonality
author: Akira Ito, Daiki Chijiwa, Atsutoshi Kumagai
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ito et al. (2026) showed that sufficiently wide, independently trained neural networks can exhibit linear mode connectivity (LMC) with softmax temperature calibration, even without permutation. LMC means that a low-loss linear path connects the models' parameters. This behavior is explained by layerwise exponentially weighted connectivity (LEWC), whereby each merged layer outputs an exponentially weighted sum of the original models' corresponding representations, yielding ensemble-like predictions. However, prior work observed LEWC with substantial widening, such as 8192 units per hidden layer for MLPs and $16\times$ width for VGG-11, raising the question of whether such widths are necessary. We therefore search for permutations that encourage reciprocal orthogonality (RO), which suppresses interference between each model's weights and the other model's representations. This allows both models' computations to coexist in the merged network, promoting LEWC at smaller widths. We formulate the search as independent layerwise quadratic assignment problems and approximately solve their continuous relaxations using Frank--Wolfe. Experiments show that our method facilitates LMC with less width expansion. It also merges models trained on different data distributions, where weight matching, which maximizes weight similarity through permutations, struggles. The merged predictions approximate those of a logit ensemble of the original models.

title: Explanation-Aware Fairness Beyond Output Parity: Joint Output-Attribution Regularization for Medical Image Classification
author: G\"okhan \"Ozbulak, Oscar Jimenez-del-Toro, Lilian Berton, Andr\'e Anjos
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Output-level fairness does not constrain whether demographic groups rely on similar predictive contributions in representation space. For a nonlinear encoder with a linear head, we show that outcome-conditioned output score disparity equals the signed sum of feature attribution differences across subgroups by allowing small prediction gaps to arise through cancellation effect. We test whether an attribution disparity penalty complements output-level equalized odds based fairness surrogates. Across 960 DINOv2-LoRA models on HAM10000 and Harvard-GF datasets for gender and race fairness, attribution augmentation increases utility-fairness trade-off performance for hypervolume in six different settings with paired 95% confidence intervals and relative gains of 1.49-10.57%. Under a predefined utility constraint, augmented model families also achieve 9.0-38.7% lower equalized odds difference, lower attribution disparity, and reduced cancellation ratio while preserving predictive utility. These results support attribution fairness as a complementary explanation-aware constraint on output fairness.

title: Continuous-Time Set-Transformers for Asynchronous WiFi-IMU Indoor Localization
author: Mohamed Bachar (LINEACT), Ilyass Abouelaziz (LINEACT), Yuehua Ding (LINEACT)
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Indoor localization commonly combines WiFi received signal strength indicator (RSSI) fingerprints with inertial measurements. However, these sensor streams are sampled asynchronously at different rates; therefore, observations rarely align in time and may be missing or stale. Most existing methods resample the data onto a shared clock and process each modality using a separate branch. We instead present a continuous-time transformer that represents observations as an unordered set of timestamped tokens. Each token encodes its measurement, modality, and elapsed time since acquisition. A single attention block jointly fuses information across modalities and time, avoiding both resampling and modality-specific branches while remaining invariant to token order. During training, we randomly mask entire modalities and individual observations, enabling the model to operate under missing or outdated inputs. We validate the modality-specific encoders on their respective benchmarks and evaluate the fused model on both simulated and real datasets, including a crosssession dataset collected on unseen days. The proposed approach improves upon an open WiFi fingerprinting baseline under cross-session drift, remains competitive with learned fusion and dead-reckoning baselines, and degrades gracefully as observations become missing or stale. These results suggest that a single continuoustime transformer provides a practical framework for indoor localization from asynchronous sensors.

title: INTENT: Out-of-Sample, Out-of-Time, and Cold-Start Evaluation on User Event Sequences
author: Mattias Kvist, Erik Lidman Hillbom, Edoardo de Cal, Davis Siemens, Adam Fredriksson, Rickard Br\"uel-Gabrielsson
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Banks now train foundation models on ordered sequences of customer events such as transactions, app sessions, and authorizations. Deployed, such a model predicts forward in time, often for customers and merchants absent from training, yet each is evaluated on private data, so no two can be compared. Public benchmarks for such sequences rarely test a period the model has not seen; recommendation studies usually hold out each user's last events instead. We present INTENT (INTEraction, Novelty, and Transfer evaluation for next-action prediction), a public benchmark that scores a model in seven cells defined by whether the user, the period, and the target item appeared in training. An audit of 59 public dataset families retains five datasets; the most common defect is the lack of a calendar timestamp that orders events. No date lies within the time span of all five datasets, so each is split at its own cutoff, chosen by one rule fixed before any model is evaluated. Summed over the datasets, every cell holds at least 111,769 users. In reference results the cell determines the best model: a transformer leads on seen items after the cutoff but scores zero on new items, a variant that embeds item metadata helps mainly on MicroLens, and repeating the user's last item leads on new items in four of five datasets. This parameter-free control also shows that on three datasets most of the score lost after the cutoff reflects changed behavior rather than the model. The pipeline, the cutoff rule, and the per-cell user counts are publicly available.

title: IC-GNN: Modeling Individualized Brain Community Organization for Disease Prediction
author: Yang Zhang, Xiao Zhou, Jonathan Warrell, Avram Holmes, Xuan Zhang, Mark Gerstein, for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Brain networks exhibit modular organization, where community structures vary substantially across individuals and diseases. Understanding these individual differences is crucial for advancing both basic neuroscience research and precision medicine. However, widely used predefined group-level brain atlases often overlook this heterogeneity. While individualized functional parcellations capture subject-specific variability in community boundaries, they often require lengthy scan times to achieve fine-grained resolution and complicate cross-subject comparisons. To address this trade-off and investigate how individualized community organization captures disease-associated changes across individuals, we propose IC-GNN, an atlas-anchored model that forms distinct, individualized functional communities directly over atlas-defined brain regions. IC-GNN derives discrete, individualized multiscale communities from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, refines community-guided connections, and adapts shared regional weights to each subject's community context to enable both individualized modeling and group-level comparisons. Across more than 30,000 participants from ABIDE (autism spectrum disorder), ADNI (Alzheimer's disease), and the UK Biobank (depression), IC-GNN achieves the highest performance compared with 15 baseline methods. We further demonstrate that these individualized communities are reproducible within scans and across sessions, and carry predictive power on their own. Furthermore, IC-GNN identifies disease-related shifts in community organization that align with established literature, highlighting a promising approach for modeling individualized community structure for disease prediction and biomarker discovery.

title: One Temperature to Rule Them All?
author: Aviv Orly (School of Physics and Astronomy, Tel Aviv University, Israel), Ori Shem-Ur (School of Physics and Astronomy, Tel Aviv University, Israel), Yaron Oz (School of Physics and Astronomy, Tel Aviv University, Israel)
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inference-time sampling is a central mechanism for improving large language models, with temperature controlling the tradeoff between reliability and diversity. While recent work suggests that varying temperature across samples can improve multi-sample inference, simple fixed-temperature schemes remain the standard in practice. We investigate this discrepancy in the canonical pass@K setting, asking when temperature diversity is useful, and when a single tuned temperature suffices. To this end, we analyze per-question success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, tracking how they vary with sampling temperature. We identify several consistent properties of these profiles, including that harder questions are less likely to share efficient sampling temperatures, although this trend is only logarithmic in hardness. We then derive an efficient method for evaluating the theoretically optimal multi-temperature allocation scheme, and show that although such a scheme improves performance, its gains over single-temperature baselines are typically modest when temperature is tuned as a function of the sampling budget K. We explain this phenomenon through mathematical mechanisms that we call dulling effects, and show how they ensure the robustness of temperature choices across different question distributions. Our results clarify when multi-temperature sampling is useful, and how temperatures should ideally be chosen.

title: Which Successes Make Good References? Action-Sequence Alignment for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
author: Mufei Li, Nikki Lijing Kuang, Zhuoer Wang, Samson Koelle, Jie Yuan, Manqing Mao, Hong Wang, Yanjun Lin, James Feng, Daniel Edmiston, Pan Li, Wei Niu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.13135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) reduces train-inference distribution mismatch by supervising a student on its own trajectories. For multi-turn tool-use agents, conditioning the teacher on a validated same-task successful trajectory as a reference can provide useful hindsight, but different successes may reach incompatible interaction states and offer misleading supervision. We cast successful-reference selection as a free-target optimal transport problem, which reduces to assigning each failed trajectory its most compatible successful reference. Because latent state paths are hidden, we use action-sequence alignment as an observable proxy for compatibility and instantiate it with longest common subsequence (LCS), which identifies a shared ordered backbone of actions while allowing recoverable detours. This perspective makes trajectory compatibility the central criterion for reference selection in multi-turn OPD. Experiments on ALFWorld and the airline domain of $\tau^3$-bench show that LCS is the only evaluated reference selector to improve over reference-free OPD on both ALFWorld overall scores and all three airline metrics. Without further optimization, the airline-trained models also transfer to the retail domain, where LCS improves all three metrics.

title: Fish Audio Releases Live 3, a Full-Duplex Voice Model That Reacts in 186 ms
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Fish Audio has released Live 3 , a full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents. The Fish Audio Live 3 full-duplex voice model keeps listening while it speaks. That lets a caller pause, say “mm-hmm,” or change their mind without breaking the call. For developers, the pitch is simple. Turn-taking moves out of hand-tuned pipeline rules and into the speech model. TL;DR Product: A full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents Runs on: Hosted Fish Agent Platform and Fish Audio API; on-premises for enterprises. Performance: Fish Audio shows behavior demos, but publishes no benchmark scores. Best: Can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms for short reactions like “mm-hmm.” What is Fish Audio Live 3? Live 3 is a full-duplex voice model from Fish Audio that listens and speaks at the same time. The core argument is that speed and timing are different problems. An agent can reply fast and still speak at the wrong moment. A pause after “What time do you open?” usually ends a turn. A pause in the middle of a phone number does not. How does Live 3 handle turn-taking? Most voice agents split recognition, reasoning, speech generation and turn-taking across separate pipeline stages. Fish Audio team states that Live 3 moves conversational timing into the speech model. It was trained on real human conversations to learn when to acknowledge, wait, respond or stop. They framed the old approach as piling on “more rules and more thresholds.” Fish Audio instead wants the model to learn timing from data. A separate reasoning layer still holds the agent’s instructions and tools. The Fish Audio team walks through 3 behaviors: Acknowledging without taking over. A caller reads “415… 555… 0132.” Live 3 may say “okay, 415” between chunks, then wait. Telling a backchannel from an interruption. A caller saying “yeah” lets the agent continue. “Wait, actually, I just need Thursday” makes it stop. Waiting through corrections. For “two pizzas… no, three,” Live 3 waits instead of logging the wrong order. How fast is Live 3? Fish Audio states Live 3 can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms . That figure covers short reactions such as “mm-hmm,” “okay” and quick confirmations. The full answer is prepared in parallel. This is a floor for small reactions, not time-to-first-audio for a complete reply. Fish Audio has not published a latency distribution. Third-party tracke

title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock
author: Aris Tsakpinis
contentSnippet: Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed from Moonshot AI is now available on Amazon Bedrock . Part of Moonshot AI’s new K3.1 series, it’s a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with the same 3T-class open-weight architecture and 1-million-token context window, trained with substantially more post-training compute. According to Moonshot AI, that extra training targets long-horizon agentic work and fewer factual errors. It also improves professional tasks such as financial modeling and office documents, and coding for game engines, 3D scenes, and computer-aided design (CAD) scripts. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed generates output tokens at a higher rate and Moonshot AI reports 2–3 times the speed of Kimi K3.1 Pro. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed uses the same endpoint, APIs, and features as Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock. If you already build with Kimi K3, you can try it by changing the model ID in your existing code. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports tool calling, structured output, configurable reasoning, image input, and streaming. You can adopt Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed without changing your security posture. Your data is processed within the AWS data boundary, isn’t shared with Moonshot AI, and isn’t used to train the model. Zero data retention is always enabled for inference requests, and with zero operator access, AWS operators can’t view your prompts and completions during inference. In this post, we show you how to get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock. We also cover how to lower costs with the Flex tier, explicit prompt caching for repeated context, and how to use the model as a coding assistant in OpenCode. Get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock To try the model without writing code, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , then Playground , and select Kimi K3.1 . From code, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on the bedrock-runtime endpoint through the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and through the Amazon Bedrock Converse and Invoke APIs. We recommend the Chat Completions API. You reach the model through cross-Region inference profiles: global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 routes requests to any supported commercial AWS Region, and costs less per token than the geographic profiles. We recommend it for most workloads. us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps processing within US Regions, and in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps it within India Reg

summary.tldr:
Moonshot AI has launched Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock, an iteration of the K3.1 series built on the 3T-class open-weight architecture. The model maintains a 1-million-token context window while incorporating significantly increased post-training compute. This optimization is specifically designed to enhance performance in long-horizon agentic workflows, reduce factual hallucinations, and improve specialized tasks including financial modeling, CAD script generation, and coding for 3D game engines.

The 'Highspeed' variant delivers output token generation rates 2–3 times faster than the standard Kimi K3.1 Pro. It maintains full compatibility with existing Kimi K3 endpoints, APIs, and features, allowing developers to switch models by updating the model ID. Supported capabilities include tool calling, structured output, configurable reasoning, image input, and streaming. The deployment adheres to AWS data privacy standards, ensuring data remains within the AWS boundary, is not shared with Moonshot AI, and is not used for model training, with zero data retention and zero operator access enabled by default.

Integration is supported via the Amazon Bedrock Converse and Invoke APIs, as well as OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions APIs. Users can access the model through cross-Region inference profiles, such as 'global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1' for cost-optimized routing, or region-specific profiles like 'us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1' and 'in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1' for data residency requirements. The platform also supports cost-reduction features including the Flex tier and explicit prompt caching.
takeaways: **Architecture:** Based on a 3T-class open-weight architecture with a 1-million-token context window.
**Performance:** The Highspeed variant achieves 2–3x faster output token generation compared to the standard Kimi K3.1 Pro.
**Data Privacy:** Operates within the AWS data boundary with zero data retention and zero operator access; prompts are not used for model training.
**API Compatibility:** Supports OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions, Amazon Bedrock Converse, and Invoke APIs.
**Inference Profiles:** Offers global routing via 'global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1' and localized profiles for US and India regions.

title: Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory
author: The Register AI
contentSnippet: Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google. On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite. Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications. "An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains. The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others. Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors, which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: "Your apps have moved into Claude." "Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses." In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending ap

summary.tldr:
Anthropic has expanded its 'Artifacts' ecosystem, signaling a strategic pivot into the enterprise productivity market traditionally held by Microsoft and Google. The company introduced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, with Claude Meetings slated for imminent release. These join existing Artifact types—Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion—to form a cohesive, Claude-centric suite. Unlike traditional files, these Artifacts function as managed, interactive objects hosted within the Claude interface, accessible via sharing URLs and supporting diverse formats including .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4.

Beyond native tools, Anthropic is positioning Claude as a central platform for third-party software integration. Through new interactive connectors, partners can embed applications directly into the Claude environment, eliminating the need for tab-switching. Initial integrations include Adobe and Atlassian, with Salesforce, NetSuite, and Workday currently in beta. These integrations feature built-in skills tailored for specific roles, such as sales call preparation, financial data analysis, and HR management, effectively challenging the traditional 'platform landlord' model maintained by established tech incumbents.
takeaways: **New Artifact Types:** Anthropic added Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data to its existing suite of Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion.
**Platform Integration:** Third-party apps from Adobe, Atlassian, Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) can now be embedded directly into the Claude interface.
**Artifact Definition:** Artifacts are defined as managed, interactive containers rather than static files, supporting formats ranging from .jsx and .html to .pptx and .mp4.
**Strategic Shift:** The company is moving toward a 'landlord' model where external enterprise software functions as a tenant within the Claude ecosystem.

title: Build a daily dependency watcher with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore web search
author: Sundar Raghavan
contentSnippet: AI agents increasingly handle work that depends on what changed today, such as security advisories, product releases, prices, and regulations. A model’s training data can’t answer those questions, so agents need web search. For production use, teams also need results they can cite, and control over which sources count. They want search queries to stay inside their cloud environment because those queries often reveal internal work. The Web Search API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is now available. It gives agents and applications current web results through a single API call, signed with the AWS credentials they already use. AWS serves every query from a web index that Amazon operates, and doesn’t send it to a third-party search engine. Each result includes the page’s title, URL, publication date, and an extract relevant to the query. Requests can include or exclude domains, and limit results to a publication date range. On AWS Lambda , Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime , your agent calls the API with its execution role. There’s no search API key to store or rotate. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is also available through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. There, one administrator source policy covers every agent and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client. For LangChain developers, the AgentCore web search tool in LangChain’s AWS integration now calls the Web Search API. One function call gives an agent current, cited search results. The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as a date window, a source blocklist, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. It works with LangChain agents, with LangGraph , the orchestration framework that runs them, and with Deep Agents , which adds subagents, a virtual filesystem, and context compression. In this post, you build a daily dependency watch for a security team as a LangGraph graph on the Web Search API. Every morning, the watch checks whether anything new affects the open source packages and container base images the team ships. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel, while your code keeps the date window, the blocklist, and the search budget out of the model’s control. It checks each finding against the sources it cites and remembers what it already reported. Then you r

summary.tldr:
Amazon has launched the Web Search API within Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, providing agents with real-time web access via AWS-managed infrastructure. Unlike third-party search integrations, this service operates entirely within the AWS environment, ensuring that search queries remain private and authenticated via standard AWS execution roles rather than external API keys. The API returns structured data including page titles, URLs, publication dates, and query-relevant extracts, while supporting granular controls such as domain filtering, date range constraints, and search budget limits.

The service integrates directly with LangChain’s AWS integration, allowing developers to incorporate cited search results into LangGraph workflows and Deep Agents. Administrators can enforce global search policies via AgentCore Gateway, which applies consistent rules—such as source blocklists and temporal windows—across all agents and Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients. This architecture enables the construction of automated monitoring systems, such as daily dependency watchers, that can perform parallel research across multiple package ecosystems while maintaining strict, code-level control over the search parameters that the underlying LLM cannot override.
takeaways: **Authentication:** Uses standard AWS execution roles for API access, eliminating the need for external search API key management or rotation.
**Data Privacy:** Queries are processed through an Amazon-operated web index, ensuring search traffic does not transit to third-party search providers.
**Policy Enforcement:** AgentCore Gateway allows administrators to set immutable rules for agents, including domain blocklists, date windows, and search budget caps.
**Integration:** Native support for LangChain, LangGraph, and Deep Agents, enabling the creation of autonomous agents that perform parallel research and citation-backed reporting.

title: Meta FAIR Releases e-means: An Algorithm Beating k-means in 10x Fewer Epochs
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Meta FAIR researchers have released e-means , a drop-in replacement for Lloyd’s k-means algorithm. The e-means clustering algorithm reaches the loss Lloyd’s k-means gets in 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs . It ships in FAISS 1.16.0 under faiss.contrib.e_means . For anyone building vector indexes, quantizers or data-curation pipelines, clustering is often the slowest offline step. e-means targets exactly that step. TL;DR Size: It is an algorithm. Tested from 100K to 10 billion points, up to 16.7M clusters. Runs on: CPU or GPU, with PyTorch tensors or NumPy. Paper GPU runs use H100s. Performance: Lower loss than Lloyd’s k-means in roughly one-tenth the epochs, across 24 dataset configurations (self-reported). Best: 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedup over Flash-KMeans at equal loss. Worst: 16M-centroid runs need 64 GiB of float32 accumulators, so centroids must be sharded across GPUs. What is e-means? e-means is a mini-batch k-means algorithm from Meta FAIR that updates centroids with exponential moving averages. How does e-means work? Every k-means variant keeps a sum S and a count N per cluster. The centroid is S divided by N. Methods differ only in how S and N change. Lloyd recomputes S and N from the full dataset each iteration. MacQueen (1967) keeps adding batch statistics forever, so stale assignments never leave. e-means decays old statistics at rate α: S ← (1−α)S + αs, and the same for N. Older assignments fade, so centroids track recent data. The research team expa Lloyd is a corner case: full batch with α = 1. On DEEP, that corner sits 1.8% above the best loss. The team tested plain gradient descent as an alternative. At its best setting, it ended 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above EMA. The authors suspect EMA wins because centroids always stay inside the hull of their assigned points. What replaces hyperparameter tuning? Two fitted scaling laws set batch size B and initial step α0 from dataset size n, cluster count k and epochs T. On held-out datasets, median regret was 0.07% for the step law. The step then follows a cosine schedule from α0 to 0.1α0. What else changed? Dead-cluster revival: clusters below a size threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. Finalization: training ends on each cluster’s exact last-epoch mean. Fused GPU kernels: nearest-centroid assignment is fused, so saved epochs become saved seconds. [EMBED: e-means interactive expla

summary.tldr:
Meta FAIR has introduced e-means, a drop-in replacement for Lloyd’s k-means clustering algorithm, now available in FAISS version 1.16.0 under the namespace faiss.contrib.e_means. Designed to accelerate vector indexing and data curation pipelines, e-means utilizes exponential moving averages (EMA) to update centroids, allowing it to achieve the same loss as Lloyd’s k-means in approximately one-tenth of the epochs. The algorithm is compatible with both CPU and GPU environments, supporting PyTorch tensors and NumPy arrays, and has been validated on datasets ranging from 100,000 to 10 billion points with up to 16.7 million clusters.

Technically, e-means improves upon traditional mini-batch k-means by decaying old statistics at a rate α, ensuring centroids effectively track recent data without the stale assignment issues found in MacQueen’s method. The implementation features fused GPU kernels for nearest-centroid assignment, dead-cluster revival via splitting, and a finalization step that calculates exact means on the final epoch. Performance benchmarks across 24 configurations show a 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedup over Flash-KMeans at equivalent loss levels. For large-scale deployments, such as 16-million-centroid runs, the algorithm requires 64 GiB of float32 accumulators, necessitating centroid sharding across multiple GPUs.
takeaways: **Performance Metric:** e-means achieves target loss in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs compared to 25 epochs for Lloyd’s k-means.
**Scaling Laws:** The algorithm replaces manual hyperparameter tuning with two fitted scaling laws that determine batch size and initial step α0 based on dataset size, cluster count, and epoch count.
**Hardware Requirements:** Large-scale runs with 16M centroids require 64 GiB of float32 memory for accumulators, requiring multi-GPU sharding.
**Comparison:** e-means outperformed plain gradient descent by 1.6% on the DEEP dataset and 0.4% on the SIFT dataset.
**Implementation:** The algorithm is integrated into FAISS 1.16.0 and utilizes a cosine schedule for the decay rate α, transitioning from α0 to 0.1α0.

title: Mercor raises $750M at $20B valuation to take AI agent evaluation to enterprises
author: Duncan Riley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 17:45 EST / NOVEMBER 10 2026

Mercor raises $750M at $20B valuation to take AI agent evaluation to enterprises

Artificial intelligence training data company Mercor.io Corp. today revealed that it has raised $750 million in new funding at a $20 billion valuation.

Mercor provides the human expertise used to train and evaluate AI models, drawing on a network of more than 5 million domain experts. Most of that work so far has been for frontier AI labs. The new funding is aimed at taking it to enterprises in every industry, which Mercor argues need their own way to measure whether an AI agent can be trusted with a job.

Co-Chief Executive Brendan Foody said “every job in the economy” will need its own AI agents and that companies will need a way to train and evaluate them on their own work. Mercor spent the past two years building that infrastructure with the frontier labs. The lab business has grown fast. Foody said in a post on X in July that annualized revenue had passed $2 billion in June.

Adarsh Hiremath, Mercor’s other co-chief executive, said a model can score well on a public benchmark and still fail on “the systems, policies and edge cases that define how a specific business runs.” For each enterprise customer, Mercor builds a custom benchmark that measures models against that company’s own standards. Post-training starts from there.

Part of that post-training runs on software from Deeptune Inc. summary.tldr:
